land.text: the 'Northern and Central Italy' the RSI 'nominally exercised sovereignty in', north of the Gustav Line and without the two German Operational Zones (Alpine Foothills: Belluno, South Tyrol, Trentino; Adriatic Littoral: Udine, Gorizia, Trieste, Pola, Fiume, Ljubljana); Rome, German-held from 10 September 1943, is a 60 km circle

predecessors.note: After Badoglio's armistice of 8 September 1943 'Germany seized' much of Italy; the Italian state of the South continued as the Kingdom of Italy. Cliopatria's Kingdom of Italy row has a 267 km2 shape for 1944, which is wrong; the eu-13 dossier owns that row.

land.text: the infobox names the Kingdom of Italy as successor; the territory north of the Gothic Line returned to the Italian state in April-May 1945

successors.note: 'In Italy, the day is known as Liberation Day' (25 April 1945).

capitals.name: Salò
capitals.note: Infobox: 'Salò, Verona, and Milan (de facto); Rome (de jure)'. Salò was the de facto seat of the government; ministries were spread around Lake Garda, Verona and Milan.

rulers.name: Benito Mussolini
rulers.title: Head of State and Prime Minister (Duce)
rulers.note: 'Its head was Benito Mussolini.' The German plenipotentiary Rudolf Rahn (1943-1945) held real power per the page. Captured and killed by partisans on 28 April 1945, three days after the government's end date.

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe, Cliopatria has no shape for the RSI (its Kingdom of Italy row shows 455,534 km2 for 1943 and 267 km2 for 1944). The page gives no area (page silent); the resolved spec is about 142,000 km2. The page says the RSI 'claimed sovereignty over all of Italy and its colonies' but its 'de facto jurisdiction only extended to a vastly reduced portion of the country'. Regions are read from the Gustav Line 'between Monte Cassino and the western seaboard' (Italian campaign page), which the page does not trace by town, so Lazio south of Rome and Abruzzo are left out as an approximation. This is also the shape of Jan-May 1944.

correction.text: north of the Gothic Line, which 'ran from the coast some 50 kilometres (30 miles) north of Pisa' to 'just south of Rimini': the Po valley, Liguria and Emilia-Romagna, without the Operational Zones

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe for the Gothic Line stage: Rome fell 4 June 1944, Ancona 18 July, Florence in August (ledger); the Gothic Line held from the Pisa coast to Rimini until the Allied offensive of 9 April 1945. About 97,000 km2 resolved. The shape holds from August 1944; January-May 1944 still has the 1943 shape. Whether Rimini and Romagna south of the Po were fully held in December 1944 is not on the pages.

region.text: the 'Northern and Central Italy' the RSI 'nominally exercised sovereignty in', north of the Gustav Line and without the two German Operational Zones (Alpine Foothills: Belluno, South Tyrol, Trentino; Adriatic Littoral: Udine, Gorizia, Trieste, Pola, Fiume, Ljubljana); Rome, German-held from 10 September 1943, is a 60 km circle

ledger.note: 23 September 1943: Mussolini proclaims the Italian Social Republic in German-held northern Italy. 'The Italian Social Republic was proclaimed on 23 September 1943'; Badoglio announced the armistice on 8 September and 'On 12 September, Mussolini was freed by the Germans in Operation Eiche'. The page names 'Northern and Central Italy', not provinces.

region.text: the RSI as German-controlled client state

ledger.note: September 1943: Germany holds the RSI as a client state. 'Germany seized and de facto incorporated some Italian territories'; the page describes Rudolf Rahn as the German plenipotentiary with real power; the nazi-germany dossier records the same land as occupation of the Italian state. The two German Operational Zones (the Alpine Foothills, OZAV, and the Adriatic Littoral, OZAK) were set up on 10 September 1943 (OZAK page) and are not part of this shape; the RSI page's footnote says 'Both OZAV and OZAK were still formally part of the RSI' and the OZAK page says they 'were separate from the Italian Social Republic'.

region.text: Rome and its 60 km, where 'American forces took possession of Rome on 4 June 1944'

ledger.note: 4 June 1944: Rome falls to the Allies. 'The American forces took possession of Rome on 4 June 1944.' Rome had been the RSI's claimed de jure capital; Salò the de facto one.
18 July 1944: Ancona falls. The page says 'succeeded in capturing it on 18 July' without a year in that passage; its context (Eighth Army advance after Rome) is 1944.

region.text: the land between Rome and the Gothic Line: Umbria, the Marche and Tuscany south of the line, including Florence

ledger.note: August 1944: the Allies reach the Gothic Line. 'From June to August 1944, the Allies advanced beyond Rome, taking Florence'. Umbria, the rest of the Marche and Tuscany south of the line pass to the Allied-held Kingdom of Italy; the page dates only Rome, Ancona and 'June to August'.

region.text: the Apennine belt of the Gothic Line, from the coast north of Pisa to just south of Rimini

ledger.note: 25 August 1944: Operation Olive attacks the Gothic Line, which 'ran from the coast some 50 kilometres (30 miles) north of Pisa' to 'just south of Rimini'. The page's Operation Olive text begins on 25 August and describes penetrations 'without a decisive breakthrough'. The line then stood through the winter ('The Allied offensive was halted in early 1945 due to poor winter weather').

region.text: the Apennine belt of the Gothic Line, from the coast north of Pisa to just south of Rimini

ledger.note: 9-21 April 1945: the Allied spring offensive breaks the line. 'The Allies' final offensive commenced with massive aerial and artillery bombardments on 9 April 1945'; 'On 21 April, Bologna was entered by the 3rd Carpathian Division'.

29 April - 2 May 1945: German forces in Italy surrender. 'signed the instrument of surrender of German forces in Italy on 29 April'; 'Army Group C surrendered unconditionally to the Allies on 2 May 1945'. The RSI page: 'On 29 April, Graziani surrendered', the RSI surrender 'was to take effect on 2 May'.

region.text: north of the Gothic Line, which 'ran from the coast some 50 kilometres (30 miles) north of Pisa' to 'just south of Rimini': the Po valley, Liguria and Emilia-Romagna, without the Operational Zones

ledger.note: 25 April 1945: the Italian Social Republic ends. 'The Government of the Italian Social Republic held office from 23 September 1943 until 25 April 1945'; 'Mussolini was captured and killed by Italian partisans on 28 April'; 'In Italy, the day is known as Liberation Day'. The infobox lists the Kingdom of Italy as successor.

wars.name: Italian campaign (World War II)

zones.text: the Apennine belt of the Gothic Line, from the coast north of Pisa to just south of Rimini

wars.outcome: The Allies take Rome (4 June 1944), Ancona (18 July) and Florence (August), stall at the Gothic Line through the winter, and break through from 9 April 1945; German forces in Italy surrender on 29 April, effective 2 May 1945.
wars.note: Front by year: Gustav Line from the Monte Cassino sector to the western seaboard in winter 1943-44 (the page gives no towns and no dates for it); Gothic Line from north of Pisa to just south of Rimini from August 1944 to April 1945.

certainty.note: The southern edge of the RSI is a moving front, which the pages describe by named lines only; the northern edge follows the pre-war frontiers with France, Switzerland and the Reich (sharp) and the borders of the two German Operational Zones (set 10 September 1943, provinces named, not surveyed).

sources.title: Italian Social Republic
sources.note: Identity, proclamation 23 September 1943, de facto capital Salò, Mussolini, German zones, end 25 April 1945, surrender 29 April / 2 May. No area figure.

sources.title: Italian campaign (World War II)
sources.note: Rome 4 June 1944, Ancona 18 July, Florence by August, Gothic Line extent, 9 April and 21 April 1945, surrender 29 April and 2 May 1945. No towns for the Gustav Line.

sources.title: Operational Zone of the Adriatic Littoral
sources.note: OZAK set up 10 September 1943 with the provinces Udine, Gorizia, Trieste, Pula, Rijeka and Ljubljana; twin OZAV of Belluno, South Tyrol and Trentino; both 'separate from the Italian Social Republic'.

notes: Cliopatria lacks the RSI; its Kingdom of Italy row has 455,534 km2 in 1943, 267 km2 in 1944 (wrong) and 289,198 km2 in 1945. Pages disagree on the Operational Zones: the RSI page's footnote has them 'still formally part of the RSI', the OZAK page says 'separate'; the shape follows the de facto line and leaves them out. They need dossiers or a nazi-germany occupation record (OZAK: Udine, Gorizia, Trieste, Pola, Fiume, Ljubljana, from 10 September 1943, Friedrich Rainer; OZAV: Belluno, Bolzano, Trento). The RSI page gives no area or population; the Gustav Line is traced only as 'between Monte Cassino and the western seaboard'. Rome was German-held from 10 September 1943 ('Rome fell to the Germans'); the RSI never governed it, so the 60 km circle in the 1943 shape is generous. The nazi-germany dossier records the RSI land as occupation of kingdom-of-italy, not as a vassal_start for italian-social-republic; the eu-21 reviewer may want the second form added there. The Kingdom of the South ('informally known as the Kingdom of the South') belongs to the kingdom-of-italy dossier (eu-13). Abruzzo, southern Lazio and the Sangro front are not named on the pages and are outside the shape.
